:::{#thm-definite-eigenvalues}
#### Definiteness and eigenvalues

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ symmetric matrix with real entries,
with eigendecomposition $\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}$
(@def-eigendecomposition)
and eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p$
on the diagonal of $\matr{\Lambda}$.
Then:

- $\matr{A}$ is positive semidefinite (@def-positive-semidefinite)
  if and only if every $\lambda_i \ge 0$.
- $\matr{A}$ is positive definite (@def-positive-definite)
  if and only if every $\lambda_i > 0$.

:::

::: proof

For any vector $\vx$ of length $p$, let $\vecf{y} = \tp{\matr{Q}}\vx$.
Then:

$$
\ba
\tp{\vx}\matr{A}\vx
&= \tp{\vx}\matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}\vx
&& \text{(substitute the eigendecomposition)}
\\
&= \tp{\paren{\tp{\matr{Q}}\vx}}\matr{\Lambda}\paren{\tp{\matr{Q}}\vx}
&& \text{(transpose of a product)}
\\
&= \tp{\vecf{y}}\matr{\Lambda}\vecf{y}
&& \text{(definition of } \vecf{y} \text{)}
\\
&= \sumip \lambda_i y_i^2
&& \text{(} \matr{\Lambda} \text{ is diagonal)}
\ea
$$

The second step is @thm-transpose-product.
Also, $\vx = \vzero$ exactly when $\vecf{y} = \vzero$:
$\matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{I}_p$ for an orthogonal matrix
(@def-orthogonal-matrix),
so $\vx = \matr{Q}\vecf{y}$.

*If every $\lambda_i \ge 0$*, then every term $\lambda_i y_i^2 \ge 0$,
so $\tp{\vx}\matr{A}\vx \ge 0$.
*If every $\lambda_i > 0$* and $\vx \neq \vzero$,
then some $y_i \neq 0$,
so at least one term is positive and the rest are non-negative,
and $\tp{\vx}\matr{A}\vx > 0$.

*Conversely*, take $\vx = \vecf{q}_i$, column $i$ of $\matr{Q}$,
which is not $\vzero$ because it has norm 1.
Then $\vecf{y} = \tp{\matr{Q}}\vecf{q}_i$ is column $i$ of $\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q} = \matr{I}_p$,
so $y_i = 1$ and every other entry of $\vecf{y}$ is $0$,
and the display gives $\tp{\vecf{q}_i}\matr{A}\vecf{q}_i = \lambda_i$.
So if $\matr{A}$ is positive semidefinite, $\lambda_i \ge 0$,
and if $\matr{A}$ is positive definite, $\lambda_i > 0$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-definite-eigenvalues}
#### Reading definiteness off the eigenvalues

- $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
  has eigenvalues $3$ and $1$ (@exm-eigenvalue),
  both positive, so it is positive definite.
- $\matr{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
  has eigenvalues $2$, for the eigenvector $(1, 1)$,
  and $0$, for the eigenvector $(1, -1)$,
  so it is positive semidefinite but not positive definite,
  as @exm-positive-definite found directly.

:::
